title.narrative: Enforcing Chiefly Accountability, Farmer Rights, and Water Justice: Strategic Litigation in Ghana’s Galamsey-Affected Cocoa Belt

description.narrative:
Ghana’s cocoa belt is being destroyed by illegal small-scale mining (galamsey). Cocoa farms cultivated over generations are excavated, rivers that supply drinking and irrigation water are poisoned with mercury and cyanide, and the farmers who hold customary rights in the land, a striking number of them women, are dispossessed without consent, consultation or compensation. Behind each dispossession sits a chain of institutional failure: stool land is reallocated for mining without the certifications and revenue controls the 1992 Constitution requires, and the state institutions charged with policing those controls, above all the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands (OASL), remain passive.
This project will bring two composite test cases in the High Court of Ghana to enforce the public duties of the state institutions responsible for stool land governance, environmental protection and water resources. The respondents will be state institutions: the OASL, the Lands Commission, the Minerals Commission, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Water Resources Commission (WRC), together with the Attorney-General. The litigation deliberately does not proceed against chiefs or traditional authorities. It instead asks the courts to define and enforce the constitutional and statutory duties of the institutions that were created precisely to prevent the abuses now occurring, and to order those institutions to act. Each case will combine three strands: institutional accountability for stool land governance under Article 267 of the Constitution, the Office of the Administrator of Stool Lands Act, 1994 (Act 481) and the Land Act, 2020 (Act 1036); enforcement of farmers’ rights to property, work, food and livelihood under Articles 18, 24, 33(3) and 36, with particular attention to the dispossession of women farmers; and the right to clean water, engaging the statutory enforcement duties of the WRC and the EPA.
Alongside the litigation, the project will train community paralegals in two to three target communities, generate published environmental evidence of contamination and land loss, and feed its findings into national policy processes. A specific legislative output is a reasoned memorandum to Parliament in the ongoing consultations on the Intestate Succession Bill, drawing on the project’s documentation of women who have lost cocoa farms through arbitrary reallocation to miners, to argue for stronger protection of spouses’ and dependants’ interests in agricultural land.
The overall goal is that cocoa-farming communities in galamsey-affected areas enjoy secure land rights, safe water and accountable stool land governance, protected by enforceable public duties of state institutions. The project pursues four objectives:
• Establish judicial precedent defining and enforcing the public duties of the OASL, the Lands Commission, the Minerals Commission, the EPA and the WRC in respect of stool land allocations for mining and the resulting environmental harm. • Vindicate the constitutional rights of affected cocoa farmers, with particular attention to women farmers dispossessed through arbitrary reallocation, and secure concrete interim and final relief for the target communities. • Build a durable community-level evidence and paralegal capacity that outlasts the project. • Convert the litigation record into legislative and policy influence, including a reasoned memorandum to Parliament in the ongoing consultations on the Intestate Succession Bill.
